item.title: ‘Bismillah, it's the darkness’: How a suspected police infiltration became a protest meme in France
item.description:
‘Bismillah, it's the darkness’: How a suspected police infiltration became a protest meme in France

Submitted by Imene Guiza on Fri, 10/16/2026 - 12:00
The viral slogan has become a symbol of student protests across the country, mocking suspected police infiltration and racial stereotypes
French high school and university students hold a poster reading "Bismillah c'est les tenebres" (Bismillah, it's darkness) during a demonstration in Nantes, France on 15 October 2026 (Stephane Mahe/Reuters)
Off

A phrase mocking an alleged attempt by police to infiltrate student protest groups has become a viral slogan in France, appearing on placards, in social media videos and across demonstrations.

“Bismillah, c’est les tenebres” has spread rapidly since early October, turning an unverified Snapchat message into a symbol of the ongoing student protests and the racial stereotypes protesters say it exposes.

The phrase originated in a screenshot of a message attributed to a user called “Mamadou”, apparently seeking information about a planned school blockade.

“Hey, bismillah, it’s the darkness. When’s the school blockade, bro, wallah?” the message read. 

Other similar messages were reportedly posted by accounts using names typically associated with people with North and West African heritage.

“Bismillah” is an Arabic expression meaning “in the name of God”, commonly used by Muslims before beginning an everyday activity. Paired with “c’est les tenebres” (“it’s the darkness” ), the phrase makes little sense.

« Bismillah c’est les ténèbres » : cette expression qui n’a absolument aucun sens aurait été utilisée par des policiers pour s’infiltrer dans des boucles snapchat avant de se faire démasquer. Devenue la risée des lycéens en colère, l’expression est largement présente sur les pancartes pendant les manifestations. #bismillah #lycées

— Jeanne Baron (@jeannebarontv) October 13, 2026

Translation: "Bismillah, it's the darkness": this expression, which makes absolutely no sense whatsoever, was reportedly used by police officers to infiltrate Snapchat group chats before getting exposed. Having become the laughingstock of angry high schoolers, the expression is widely featured on placards during the protests.

Its awkward mixture of Arabic expressions, stereotypical slang and references to North African identity led students to suspect the account belonged to a police officer posing as a teenager to gain access to private protest groups.

The account’s identity has not been independently verified.

From screenshot to street slogan

The Snapchat screenshot quickly inspired parodies mocking what students saw as a clumsy attempt to imitate Gen Z’s online language. Critics also pointed to the message’s use of an African name, Algerian flag emojis and Arabic expressions as a caricature of young people of African descent.

The phrase soon spread from Snapchat to TikTok, Instagram and X, appearing on protest placards and in videos from school blockades and demonstrations.

@hologramme8

« Bismillah c'est les ténèbres » n'est pas une organisation ou un groupe, mais un slogan populaire (mème) apparu dans les manifestations lycéennes en France dernierement. Il ne s'agit pas d'une « organisation des ténèbres », mais d'une phrase absurde née de la moquerie envers la police. Pendant les mouvements de blocage des lycées, des lycéens ont rapporté sur Snapchat avoir reçu des messages de comptes inconnus tentant de s'infiltrer dans des groupes privés pour obtenir des informations sur les blocages. Ces messages prétendaient imiter le langage des jeunes des quartiers, mais leur maladresse a immédiatement éveillé les soupçons. Les internautes ont massivement supposé qu'il s'agissait de policiers en civil tentant de s'infiltrer. Parmi les captures d'écran devenues virales, un message d'un certain « Mamadou » disait : « Salut ! Bismillah c'est les ténèbres. C'est quand le blocus wallah mon frangin. On va tous casser. ». Cette phrase absurde (où « Bismillah » signifie « au nom de Dieu ») a déclenché l'hilarité générale, car elle était considérée comme une caricature grossière des jeunes par la police. Les lycéens se sont réapproprié cette phrase, la transformant en slogan contestataire · Sur les réseaux sociaux : elle a été largement reprise dans des vidéos humoristiques et des imitations de policiers infiltrés. · Dans les manifestations : elle a été écrite sur des pancartes, devenant l'un des slogans emblématiques du mouvement lycéen de 2026. · Signification : cette phrase n'a aucun sens religieux, elle tourne en dérision la façon dont la police tente maladroitement d'imiter les minorités jeunes avec des stéréotypes raciaux, et raille l'échec de l'infiltration policière.

♬ son original - hologramme

It was also repeated by activist Greta Thunberg, who joined the protests this week. 

The slogan emerged amid a wave of student mobilisation that began in Creteil, in the suburbs of Paris, on 18 September and spread across the country. 

Students have organised blockades and demonstrations over staff shortages, overcrowded classrooms, deteriorating school facilities and insufficient educational resources. Some have also demanded changes to Parcoursup, France’s higher education admissions system.

Many have highlighted how schooling conditions disproportionately affect the country's minorities and working-class suburbs.

Protesters have grown to the hundreds of thousands across the country. Police have fired tear gas and carried out baton charges against the demonstrations, which are largely peaceful. 

As the protests have grown, memes and internet trends have become part of their visual language, used to mock authority, build solidarity and attract attention while expressing anger over their education and treatment by police.

item.title: Hamas accuses Mladenov of siding with Israel over Gaza goods dispute
item.description:
Hamas accuses Mladenov of siding with Israel over Gaza goods dispute

Hamas has rejected accusations from Board of Peace Director-General Nickolay Mladenov over halted commercial deliveries to Gaza, saying he repeated Israel’s account.

In a statement on Friday, the group dismissed his accusation of “coercion,” calling his position “blatant bias and complicity with the occupation and its pretexts aimed at obstructing the entry of goods”.

Mladenov wrote on social media on Thursday that Israel’s Coordinator of Government Activities in the Territories (COGAT) had sent him a report blaming Hamas for the suspension.

COGAT operates under Israel’s defence ministry and oversees civilian affairs in the Palestinian territories.

item.title: Iran warns US against targeting energy facilities
item.description:
Iran warns US against targeting energy facilities

Tehran has pledged swift retaliation if Washington threatens its energy infrastructure.

Iran’s acting oil minister, Hamid Bovard, said the country would respond “immediately and appropriately to any US threat to Iranian energy facilities”.

“The war that the United States started by ignoring international norms has affected the energy sector globally,” he said.

“We will take precise and appropriate retaliatory measures at the right time to counter enemy threats.”

item.title: Iranian president says his country 'will not give in to force' from US
item.description:
Iranian president says his country 'will not give in to force' from US

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian has warned that the US will not be able to make his country capitulate through force.

“Iran is not seeking nuclear weapons, and we consider the destructive propaganda against our country to be lies,” he said during a trip to Armenia.

“We have always been ready to talk; they think they can make us surrender, but we will not give in to force."

item.title: Saudi Arabia to execute man for being at protests and funerals when he was 15
item.description:
Use of death penalty against people for crimes committed when they were children a ‘new low’, say rights groups

A young man faces imminent execution in Saudi Arabia for attending protests and funerals when he was aged 15 to 17, say human rights groups, in the latest example of the kingdom’s surging use of the death penalty for non-violent crimes.

Youssef al-Manasif was arrested in 2017 and accused of crimes including joining demonstrations for religious freedom by the Shia minority and attending funerals that the Saudi authorities deem to be protests. He was convicted and sentenced to death by the specialised criminal court, a secretive tribunal set up for terrorism-related cases.

item.description:
Maeen Abdulmalik Saeed says Iran-backed militia’s use of drones represents ‘new era of radical terrorism’

  • Food and fuel run low as besieged Yemeni city braces for Houthi breakthrough

The future of western security is being fought out in the mountains and hills surrounding the south-western Yemeni city of Taiz, the country’s former prime minster has said.

Maeen Abdulmalik Saeed, now an adviser to Yemen’s president, said it would be catastrophic if the city fell to the Iran-backed Houthi rebels, since control of the strategic Bab al-Mandab strait in the Red Sea and the road to Aden – the site of the UN-recognised government – would be lost.
